item: The RAM model: a single processor, uniform memory of cells S[0], S[1], ..., a constant number of registers, and every instruction (load, store, arithmetic, jump) costs one time step; running time = number of instructions executed.

Word-size convention: a cell holds a w-bit word with w >= log n (usually w >= log S for space S), because a word must be able to hold a pointer/array index; integers polynomial in the input size fit in O(1) words.

Why words must be bounded: with unbounded unit-cost integers, n repeated squarings build a 2^n-bit number in n steps, giving absurdly optimistic algorithms (and P = NP with multiplication and shifts), so the word size is tied to the input size.

Big numbers are not unit cost: an integer of k bits occupies about k/w words and arithmetic on it costs time growing with k/w; spreading a value over logarithmically many cells costs only a logarithmic overhead, which is why constant-size and log-size cell models are interchangeable up to that factor.

Transdichotomous RAM (Fredman-Willard): the word size scales with the problem size, w >= log n, and a fixed set of operations each touching O(1) cells; words double as pointers, so memory is addressed arbitrarily.
Unit-cost operations on the word RAM are the C-style ones: + - * / % & | ^ << >> and comparisons, each O(1) on a w-bit word; this is the standard model for integer data structures.

Multiplication is the contested operation: it is not in AC0 (needs depth growing with w), so the AC0 RAM allows only addition, shifts and bitwise ops; fusion trees rely heavily on multiplication, and AC0-only search results are weaker.
The RAM's key power over the comparison model: it can use keys to compute addresses (indexing, bucketing, bit extraction), which is exactly what bucket and radix sort exploit.

Integer keys cover more than integers: floating-point numbers order correctly when their bit patterns are read as integers (for negatives the bits must be flipped first, a detail the source leaves out), so integer-key algorithms apply to many other key types.

Comparison-sorting lower bound: any comparison-based sort needs n log n - O(n) comparisons worst case and on average; it cannot be broken within that model, only by enlarging the set of basic operations.
Counting/bucket sort (KSort) sorts n keys in 0..K-1 in O(n + K) and is stable; LSD radix sort applies it digit by digit for keys in 0..K^d - 1 in O(d(n + K)), relying on stability for correctness.
placement: counting/radix/bucket sort in a later chapter

item: Radix sort on the word RAM: with digit size log n bits, w-bit keys sort in O(n * w / log n) time, i.e. linear when w = O(log n); counting sort alone is O(n + 2^w).

State of integer sorting: signature sort is linear for w = Omega(log^(2+eps) n); Han gives O(n log log n) deterministic; Han-Thorup O(n sqrt(log log n)) randomized; whether O(n) sorting is possible for all w is open.
Thorup's equivalence: sorting n w-bit integers in O(n S(n,w)) time yields a priority queue with O(S(n,w)) per operation, so integer sorting and integer priority queues are tied.

Predecessor problem: maintain a set of integers from universe U = {0..u-1} under insert/delete and find predecessor/successor; it requires Theta(log n) in the BST/comparison model, which integer structures beat.
van Emde Boas trees: recursive sqrt(u) split into clusters plus a summary, min stored non-recursively so each operation recurses once: T(u) = T(sqrt u) + O(1) = O(log log u) = O(log w).

vEB space is Theta(u), not Theta(n); replacing cluster arrays with dynamic perfect hash tables (storing only non-empty clusters) brings space to Theta(n) with O(log log u) bounds holding with high probability.

x-fast and y-fast tries (Willard): a hash table of all prefixes of stored keys allows binary search on prefix length in O(log w); indirection with Theta(w)-size BST buckets gives y-fast tries O(log w) operations in O(n) space.

Word-RAM hashing is itself a word-level trick: multiply-shift hashing (multiply by a random odd word, keep the high bits) is universal up to a factor 2 and far faster than mod-prime hashing; vEB/y-fast space bounds depend on such hashing.
Fusion trees (Fredman-Willard): a B-tree of branching factor w^(1/5) where each node's keys are sketched into one word and compared in parallel, giving predecessor in O(log_w n) time with O(n) space.

Fusion-tree ingredients are word-level parallelism: sketching (compressing keys to their distinguishing bits via multiplication), parallel comparison of many small fields in one word, and computing the most significant set bit in O(1).

Combining vEB and fusion trees gives O(min{log w, log_w n}), which is at most O(sqrt(log n)); exponential search trees make this dynamic, reaching the optimal O(sqrt(log n / log log n)) worst case in linear space.
Cell-probe model (Yao): memory of w-bit cells, only reads/writes cost, computation is free; it is stronger than the word RAM, so its lower bounds hold for any RAM algorithm.

Predecessor lower bounds: with polynomial space, Omega(min{log_w n, log w / log log n}) cell probes are needed (Beame-Fich, round elimination), and Patrascu-Thorup give the exact time-space trade-off, so vEB and fusion trees are essentially optimal.
Predecessor and external memory: the fusion-tree branch log_w n matches B-tree behaviour, and with cells of B keys the optimum is either a B-tree or the best RAM structure (Patrascu-Thorup).
What unit cost hides, memory: a RAM has uniform memory, a real machine a hierarchy; a main-memory access can cost hundreds of times a cache hit, so operation costs are not fixed.
What unit cost hides, address translation: TLB misses force page-table walks; access patterns touching many pages slow down even when cache-line counts are equal.

What unit cost hides, branch mispredictions: data-dependent comparisons (e.g. in quicksort partitioning) cause mispredictions that dominate running time; separating control flow from data flow speeds sorting by over 80%.
Branch-free and prefetch-friendly search: conditional moves and the Eytzinger layout make comparison search much faster in practice than layouts with the same RAM cost.

What unit cost hides, SIMD and instruction-level parallelism: 128-512-bit vector registers process many items per instruction (e.g. AVX2 popcount up to twice as fast as the scalar popcnt instruction); the word RAM models only one w-bit word per step.
What unit cost hides, parallelism: multicore, SMT, GPUs and distributed systems; the sequential RAM gives no single simple model for these.
What unit cost hides, memory allocation: malloc/free are treated as O(1) but real allocators trade locality, contention and fast paths, and allocator choice measurably changes performance.

Real-world relevance: in-place radix sort (IPS2Ra) wins on near-uniform keys and small keys, yet a tuned branchless comparison samplesort (IPS4o) often beats integer sorters, so asymptotic wins over the comparison model depend on the hidden costs.
